subtopic_name: Introduction to the Particulate Nature of Matter

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a compound?

options.feedback: O₂ is an element, not a compound. It's made of one type of atom (oxygen), even though each molecule has 2 atoms.
Correct! NaCl contains two different elements (sodium and chlorine) chemically bonded in a fixed ratio.
Fe is an element, not a compound. It contains only one type of atom.
Air is a mixture of gases (N₂, O₂, Ar, CO₂). The components are not chemically bonded.

questions.question_text: A student heats a white solid and it completely decomposes into two different colored gases. The white solid was most likely:

options.feedback: Elements cannot decompose into different substances. Decomposition requires breaking chemical bonds.
Mixtures separate by physical methods (heating, filtering, distillation) into their original components — they don't decompose into NEW substances.
Correct! Decomposition (a chemical process producing NEW substances) indicates a compound breaking into elements or simpler compounds.
An alloy is a mixture of metals. Heating wouldn't cause the dramatic decomposition described.

questions.question_text: During the melting of ice at 0°C, what happens to the kinetic energy and potential energy of the water molecules?

options.text: Both kinetic and potential energy increase
options.feedback: At constant temperature (0°C), kinetic energy stays constant. Only potential energy increases as intermolecular forces are overcome.

options.text: Kinetic energy stays constant, potential energy increases
options.feedback: Correct! During phase change at constant temperature, energy input breaks intermolecular forces (potential energy) without increasing particle speed (kinetic energy).

options.text: Kinetic energy increases, potential energy stays constant
options.feedback: If kinetic energy increased, temperature would increase. But we're AT 0°C — the temperature doesn't change during melting.

options.text: Both kinetic and potential energy stay constant
options.feedback: If neither changed, why would the ice melt? Energy must be going somewhere — it's breaking intermolecular bonds.

questions.question_text: When you first start heating water at room temperature, you see small bubbles forming at the bottom of the container. What are these bubbles?

options.text: Water vapor (gaseous H₂O) being produced by boiling
options.feedback: The water isn't hot enough to boil yet. These bubbles form at room temperature.

options.text: Air that was dissolved in the water, escaping as it warms
options.feedback: Correct! Water naturally dissolves gases from air. As temperature increases, dissolved gases escape. Later, at 100°C, vigorous bubbles of water vapor form.
Photosynthesis doesn't occur in plain water without organisms. These are dissolved gases escaping.

options.text: Water vapor being produced (it's already boiling)
options.feedback: Water only boils at 100°C. Early small bubbles at room temperature are dissolved air, not water vapor. Learn to distinguish the two.

questions.question_text: The average kinetic energy of gas particles at 300 K is E. What is the average kinetic energy at 600 K?

options.feedback: If kinetic energy didn't change, why would we say the temperature doubled? Temperature and average kinetic energy are directly proportional.
Correct! Average kinetic energy is directly proportional to Kelvin temperature. Doubling K (300 → 600) doubles the average KE.
This shows the error of using Celsius! 300°C ≈ 573 K and 600°C ≈ 873 K, which is only 1.52x, not 2x. ALWAYS use Kelvin for proportionality.
That would be correct if we SQUARED the temperature ratio. But KE ∝ T (linear), not T².
